lesson.title: SOHCAHTOA: Turning Triangle Sides Into Angle Information
lesson.summary: Sine, cosine, and tangent are ratios of a right triangle's sides, defined relative to a chosen angle, that let you connect an acute angle to the lengths around it whenever you know just a little information about the triangle.
lesson.body:
The Pythagorean theorem from the last chapter relates all three sides of a right triangle to each other through a sum of squares, but it says nothing about the triangle's angles. Trigonometry fills that gap by comparing sides as ratios relative to one specific acute angle. Once you pick an angle to focus on, other than the right angle, the three sides get new, angle-dependent names: the hypotenuse is still the longest side, opposite the right angle, but the leg directly across from your chosen angle is now called the opposite side, and the leg touching your chosen angle, other than the hypotenuse, is the adjacent side. These labels are not fixed to a particular side of the triangle, they shift depending on which angle you are looking from.

The three basic trigonometric ratios, remembered with the mnemonic SOHCAHTOA, define exactly how these sides combine: sine of the angle equals opposite over hypotenuse, cosine of the angle equals adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent of the angle equals opposite over adjacent. These are genuinely just ratios, the same concept from the ratios and proportions chapter, applied specifically to the sides of a right triangle around a chosen angle.

Return to the 6, 8, 10 right triangle from the previous chapter. Suppose you focus on the acute angle for which the side of length 6 is opposite and the side of length 8 is adjacent, with the hypotenuse still 10. Then sine of that angle is 6/10, which is 0.6, cosine is 8/10, which is 0.8, and tangent is 6/8, which is 0.75. These numbers are not arbitrary either: sine squared plus cosine squared always equals 1 for any angle, and you can verify it here, 0.6 squared plus 0.8 squared is 0.36 plus 0.64, which is exactly 1. That identity is really just the Pythagorean theorem in disguise, dividing every term of 6 squared plus 8 squared equals 10 squared by 10 squared.

If you know a trig ratio but not the angle itself, a calculator's inverse trig functions, labeled sin inverse, cos inverse, and tan inverse, will reverse the process and hand back the angle measure. For the triangle above, taking the inverse sine of 0.6 gives an angle of approximately 36.9 degrees. On the ACT, trigonometry questions typically hand you two known pieces of a right triangle, either two sides or one side and an angle, and ask you to find the third, and SOHCAHTOA, together with the Pythagorean theorem when a third side is needed, is the complete toolkit for solving them.
